examShortTricks: Trick 1: Starch test order — I2 turns starch blue-black; Br2 turns starch yellow; Cl2 bleaches litmus — three colours, three identifications.
Trick 2: Chlorine water displaces Br2 (orange) and I2 (brown) from bromides/iodides — the displacement test distinguishes Cl2 from the rest.
Trick 3: AgNO3 precipitate colours: AgCl white, AgBr pale yellow, AgI yellow — dissolve in NH3: AgCl yes, AgBr partly, AgI no.
keyPoints: Cl2: bleaches moist litmus; liberates Br2/I2 from their salt solutions.
Br2: orange-brown vapour; colours starch paper yellow.
I2: blue-black with starch; violet vapour on sublimation.
practiceQuestions: Q. How will you distinguish Cl2 and I2 vapours? (2 marks) — I2 turns starch blue-black; Cl2 bleaches litmus and does not.
Q. What colour is AgBr precipitate? (1 mark) — pale yellow, partly soluble in ammonia.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: One-line comparisons — acidic strength: HF < HCl < HBr < HI (bond weaker down the group); reducing strength: HCl < HBr < HI; stability: HF > HCl > HBr > HI.
Trick 2: Preparation differences: HCl by NaCl + conc. H2SO4; HBr/HI cannot use H2SO4 (oxidised to Br2/I2) — use H3PO4 instead; that contrast is the mark.
Trick 3: HI reduces H2SO4 to SO2 and conc. HNO3 to NO2 — quote one equation as evidence of strong reducing nature.
keyPoints: HCl, HBr, HI are strong acids; HF is weak (H-bonding).
Reducing power increases and stability decreases down the group.
HBr and HI are prepared with H3PO4 because H2SO4 oxidises them.
HI reduces concentrated H2SO4 to SO2.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why is HI a stronger reducing agent than HCl? (1 mark) — weaker H–I bond; iodide is more easily oxidised.
Q. Why can HBr not be prepared from KBr and conc. H2SO4? (2 marks) — H2SO4 oxidises the HBr formed to Br2; H3PO4 (non-oxidising) is used.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: List by class — crystalline: diamond, graphite, fullerene (C60); amorphous: coal, coke, charcoal, lamp black, wood charcoal.
Trick 2: Structure contrast: diamond sp3 tetrahedral 3-D network (hardest, insulator); graphite sp3 + sp2 layered (conductor, lubricant) — the 'why' is hybridisation.
Trick 3: Fullerene C60: football/soccer-ball structure with 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons — quote 'buckminsterfullerene' for the name mark.
keyPoints: Diamond: sp3, tetrahedral network, hardest natural substance, non-conductor.
Graphite: sp2, hexagonal layers with delocalised electrons — conductor and lubricant.
Fullerene C60: closed cage of 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons.
Amorphous forms: coke, charcoal, lamp black, coal.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why does graphite conduct electricity while diamond does not? (2 marks) — graphite has delocalised π electrons between layers; diamond's valence electrons are all in σ bonds.
Q. Name the crystalline allotropes of carbon. (1 mark) — diamond, graphite, fullerene.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: CO is a reducing agent because C goes from +2 to +4: Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2 (blast furnace) — the standard equation.
Trick 2: With metals: Ni + 4CO → Ni(CO)4 (Mond's process for nickel purification); with non-metals: CO + Cl2 → COCl2 (phosgene, sunlight).
Trick 3: Toxicity one-liner: CO binds haemoglobin ~200× more strongly than O2, causing oxygen starvation (carboxyhaemoglobin).
keyPoints: CO is a strong reducing agent (reduces metal oxides in the blast furnace).
Forms metal carbonyls such as Ni(CO)4 (Mond's process).
Highly poisonous: forms stable carboxyhaemoglobin with blood.
Uses: reducing agent, fuel (water gas, producer gas), nickel refining.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why is CO poisonous? (2 marks) — binds haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen, blocking O2 transport.
Q. Write the reaction of CO with Ni and its use. (2 marks) — Ni + 4CO → Ni(CO)4; Mond's process purifies nickel.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Name them all in one breath: white (yellow), red, scarlet, violet, black — 'name only' means the list itself is the answer.
Trick 2: White vs red in two points each: white — waxy, soluble in CS2, stored under water, highly poisonous, reactive; red — polymeric, insoluble, non-poisonous, stable.
Trick 3: Conversion: white → red by heating at 250 °C in an inert atmosphere; red → white vapour at 400 °C.
keyPoints: Allotropes: white, red, scarlet, violet and black phosphorus.
White phosphorus is waxy, poisonous and reactive; stored under water.
Red phosphorus is a stable polymeric form used on match boxes.
practiceQuestions: Q. Name the allotropes of phosphorus. (1 mark) — white, red, scarlet, violet, black.
Q. Why is white phosphorus stored under water? (1 mark) — it ignites spontaneously in air.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Lab preparation: P4 + 3NaOH + 3H2O → PH3 + 3NaH2PO2 (heated, inverted flask over water) — remember the product sodium hypophosphite.
Trick 2: Purity test: pure PH3 is odourless; impure (P2H4) ignites spontaneously — 'spontaneous flaming rings' is the observation to quote.
Trick 3: Basic nature weaker than NH3: PH3 + HBr → PH4Br (phosphonium bromide) exists but phosphine is far less basic; reducing: PH3 + 3O2 → P2O5 + 3H2O... use 2PH3 + 4O2 → P2O5 + 3H2O.
keyPoints: PH3 is prepared by heating white phosphorus with NaOH solution.
It is less basic than ammonia but forms phosphonium salts with HBr/HI.
Reducing in nature; burns to P2O5 and H2O.
Impure phosphine containing P2H4 is spontaneously inflammable.
practiceQuestions: Q. Write the laboratory preparation of phosphine. (2 marks) — P4 + 3NaOH + 3H2O → PH3 + 3NaH2PO2 (heat).
Q. Why does impure PH3 catch fire in air? (1 mark) — traces of diphosphine (P2H4) ignite spontaneously.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Allotrope names: rhombic (α, octahedral, stable below 96 °C), monoclinic (β, prismatic, 96–119 °C), plastic (γ, amorphous) + milk of sulphur and colloidal sulphur.
Trick 2: Transition temperature 95.6 °C between rhombic and monoclinic — the exact number earns the mark.
Trick 3: Uses in one line each: vulcanisation of rubber, H2SO4 manufacture, gunpowder/matches, fungicides and medicines.
keyPoints: Rhombic sulphur: stable below 95.6 °C, octahedral yellow crystals.
Monoclinic sulphur: needle-shaped, stable between 95.6 °C and melting point.
Plastic (amorphous) sulphur forms by quenching boiling sulphur.
Uses: vulcanising rubber, making H2SO4, matches, gunpowder, fungicides.
practiceQuestions: Q. Name the allotropes of sulphur. (1 mark) — rhombic, monoclinic, plastic (plus colloidal/milk of sulphur).
Q. What is the transition temperature of sulphur? (1 mark) — 95.6 °C.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Kipp's equation: FeS + H2SO4(dil) → FeSO4 + H2S↑ — apparatus works by stopcock-controlled contact between acid and FeS in the middle bulb; draw the three-bulb shape.
Trick 2: Acidic nature: 2H2S ⇌ 2H+ + S2−, a weak diprotic acid — reacts with bases to give two series of salts (HS− and S2−).
Trick 3: Reducing nature equations: H2S + Cl2 → 2HCl + S (decoulourises Cl2 water); 2H2S + SO2 → 3S + 2H2O; H2S turns acidified KMnO4 colourless.
Trick 4: Analytical use: group II cation sulphides are coloured — PbS black, CdS yellow, ZnS white; 'H2S in qualitative analysis' is the use to quote.
keyPoints: H2S is prepared in Kipp's apparatus from FeS and dilute H2SO4.
Weak diprotic acid; rotten-egg smell; poisonous.
Strong reducing agent: decolourises KMnO4, reduces SO2 and halogens to sulphur.
Used in qualitative analysis to precipitate metal sulphides.
practiceQuestions: Q. Write the reaction for preparing H2S in Kipp's apparatus. (1 mark) — FeS + H2SO4 → FeSO4 + H2S.
Q. Show the reducing action of H2S with SO2. (2 marks) — 2H2S + SO2 → 3S↓ + 2H2O (yellow sulphur).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: SO2 is BOTH reducing and oxidising (S in +4, between −2 and +6): reduces KMnO4/I2; oxidises H2S to S — give one equation of each type.
Trick 2: Bleaching is TEMPORARY (reduction of the dye; colour returns on air oxidation) unlike Cl2's permanent oxidation bleaching — the contrast is the mark.
Trick 3: Acidic nature: SO2 + H2O → H2SO3 (sulphurous acid, dibasic); test: turns acidified dichromate paper green (Cr3+).
keyPoints: SO2 dissolves in water forming weak dibasic sulphurous acid.
Reducing agent: decolourises acidified KMnO4 and iodine solutions.
Oxidising agent: oxidises H2S to sulphur.
Temporary bleaching agent (reduces dyes); used in preserving fruits.
practiceQuestions: Q. Show SO2 acting as oxidising agent. (2 marks) — SO2 + 2H2S → 3S + 2H2O.
Q. Why is SO2 bleaching temporary? (1 mark) — it reduces the dye; air re-oxidises and colour returns.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Dehydrating evidence: sugar → black carbon column (C12H22O11 —11H2O→ 12C); also dehydrates formic acid to CO — the 'charring' observation scores.
Trick 2: Oxidising: Cu + 2H2SO4(conc.) → CuSO4 + SO2 + 2H2O (hot); C → CO2; S → SO2.
Trick 3: Acidic: dibasic → two salt series (sulphates and bisulphates); 'king of chemicals' — highest tonnage chemical, used in fertilisers, batteries, refining petroleum.
keyPoints: Strong dibasic acid giving sulphates and hydrogen sulphates.
Hot concentrated H2SO4 is an oxidising agent (Cu → SO2).
Powerful dehydrating and hygroscopic agent (chars sugar).
Uses: fertilisers, storage batteries, petroleum refining, dyes, explosives.
practiceQuestions: Q. Show the dehydrating nature of conc. H2SO4 with sugar. (2 marks) — C12H22O11 —(conc. H2SO4)→ 12C + 11H2O (black mass).
Q. Write the reaction of copper with hot conc. H2SO4. (2 marks) — Cu + 2H2SO4 → CuSO4 + SO2 + 2H2O.
